We face an unprecedented moment, in a time of geopolitical challenges, but also one of unprecedented momentum in the global energy transition. The transition is no longer a question of ‘if’ - but of how fast, how fairly, and how securely we can collectively achieve it. Cost-competitive renewables are a reality.
 
Great honour to launch IRENA’s "Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2024" report side by side with the United Nations in support of United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres's "Moment of Opportunity" speech today. During #HLPF, I informed Deputy Secretary-General Amina J. Mohammed of the continued cost leadership of renewables in global power markets.
 
The addition of 582 gigawatts of renewable capacity in 2024 led to significant cost savings, avoiding fossil fuel use valued at about USD 57 billion. 91% of new renewable power projects commissioned last year were more cost effective than any new fossil fuel alternatives. 
 
In total, in 2024, renewables helped avoid USD 467 billion in fossil fuel costs, reinforcing their role not only as the lowest-cost source of new power but also as a key driver of energy security, economic stability, and resilience in a volatile global energy landscape. This achievement is the result of years of innovation, policy direction, and growing markets. 
 
However, this progress is not guaranteed. Rising geopolitical tensions, trade tariffs, and material supply constraints threaten to slow the momentum and drive-up costs. To safeguard the gains of the energy transition, we must reinforce international cooperation, secure open and resilient supply chains, and create stable policy and investment frameworks. 
 
The transition to renewables is irreversible, but its pace and fairness depend on the choices we make today.

“Over 90% of new renewables worldwide produced electricity for less than the cheapest new fossil fuel alternative. This is not just a shift in power. This is a shift in possibility... We have the tools to power the future for humanity. Let’s make the most of them. This is our moment of opportunity.” - António Guterres  
 
The clean energy future is no longer a promise, it’s a fact. The latest Unitednations secretarygeneral  synthesis report, Supercharging the New Energy Era - with contributions from UNDP  and partners - captures this global momentum and sets out what’s needed to turn it into lasting, inclusive progress. The full report is available here: 👉 https://lnkd.in/e_HHrGzg 
 
In 2024, renewables accounted for over 90% of new power capacity. Solar and wind are now the most affordable options in many markets. Battery storage has increased more than 40 times since 2015. Clean energy jobs now outnumber those in fossil fuels. These are not isolated achievements; they’re signs of growing global readiness to scale sustainable energy solutions that support the SDGs. 
 
Yet we face a dual challenge: “The energy transition is unstoppable. But the transition is not yet fast enough or fair enough.” Fossil fuels still dominate supply. Less than 20% of clean energy investment reaches the Global South - where it’s needed most. To turn momentum into inclusive, sustained progress, the report outlines six priority actions to keep the 1.5°C target within reach and ensure no one is left behind. 
 
1️⃣ Align policies: Ensure coherence, clarity, and certainty by integrating energy, climate, and economic policies to accelerate a just transition. 
  
2️⃣ Build infrastructure: Modernize grids, expand storage, and develop digital and physical systems to support a 21st century clean energy economy. 
  
3️⃣ Power growth with renewables: Meet rising electricity demand - especially from AI and data centers - with clean, affordable renewable energy. 
  
4️⃣ Center people and equity for a just transition: Put communities first by ensuring fair access, job creation and inclusive development in all transition efforts. 
  
5️⃣ Expand global cooperation: Strengthen trade, investment and innovation partnerships to supercharge deployment and reduce costs worldwide. 
  
6️⃣ Unlock finance for the Global South: Dismantle barriers to affordable capital and scale energy-transition investments to $1.4–1.9 trillion annually in EMDEs. 
 
This is not only an energy imperative - it’s a development opportunity. @UNDP stands ready to help scale solutions, unlock investment, and ensure the energy transition powers progress for everyone, everywhere.

💥 Debt-for-climate and debt-for-nature swaps are often hailed as “innovative” ways to address both debt distress and development finance. In practice, they systematically underperform on both fronts. Udaibir Saran Das makes this point clearly with excellent examples in his new piece, "Do debt swaps deliver on development finance?" https://lnkd.in/e3SmeC56 His analysis highlights exactly why these debt swaps fall short and why the underlying diagnosis matters.

The underlying problem is misdiagnosed. Most developing countries are not insolvent—they are illiquid. (This is one area where I slightly diverge from Mr. Das’s analysis, which frames many countries as insolvent. But in many cases, the issue is not an inability to repay over time, but rather the mismatch between short-term debt obligations and long-term development returns.) They face debt distress not because of reckless borrowing or weak fundamentals, but because they can only access capital on terrible terms: short maturities and high interest rates. Why? Because of structurally biased credit rating methodologies that penalize countries for being poor, even when they are high-growth, creditworthy markets.

We explain these structural factors in our Columbia Center on Sustainable Investment paper on Lowering the Cost of Capital in EMDEs https://lnkd.in/eJYAh6WN (co-authored with Jeffrey Sachs Ana Maria Camelo Vega and Bradford M. Willis )

These swaps purport to unlock capital, but they don't in any way unlock the structural barriers to affordable capital. Instead, they:
• Mobilize a tiny fraction of the finance actually needed for climate or nature, let alone the Sustainable Development Goals
 • Deliver negligible debt relief 
 • Impose significant transaction costs—up to 25% of the total—largely enriching intermediaries
 • Often require offshore control structures that constrain national sovereignty
 • And, perversely, may even trigger credit downgrades or negative outlooks by rating agencies for looking too much like a default.

Debt swaps are not a credible or effective tool to address the debt crisis or to mobilize critical finance. If we are serious about solving either of those challenges, we should start by understanding the (interrelated) root causes and then focus on ensuring EMDEs have access to long-term, affordable finance, including from global capital markets.  And for existing debt, accumulated over decades under these discriminatory systems, we should at the very least restructure it to align with the long-term growth trajectories of rapidly growing EMDEs.

(Thanks to Paul DeNoon for sharing the article!).

Many countries in the Global South are actively working to advance energy transitions - even in the context of tight fiscal constraints.  

In my latest illuminem  article, I unpack the conversation on debt and the energy transition; not as parallel issues, but as deeply interconnected challenges shaping development trajectories: 🔗📘  https://lnkd.in/euFEESVQ

Reallocating a portion of the $1 trillion in global fossil fuel subsidies could create the fiscal space needed to accelerate sustainable, inclusive energy systems where they are most needed. That is why we need a different model - one that: 

➡️ Redirects fossil fuel subsidies - freeing up public funds that can better serve people and planet. 

➡️ Unlocks blended and concessional finance - to channel more of the 85% of clean energy investment not yet reaching the Global South. 

➡️ Aligns debt relief with climate ambition - easing pressure for the 54 countries that spend +10% of government budgets on debt service. 

➡️ Invests in long-term resilience - so regions like Africa, needing $200B annually for clean energy, can tap into the resources that they need. 

Debt is no longer just a macroeconomic indicator; it is shaping what is possible in energy, in equity, and in development. 

Getting this right isn’t just urgent. It’s foundational.

What if the world’s smallest island nations became the world's leaders in AI-powered clean energy? 🏝️⚡️ 
 
Small Island Developing States (SIDS) are redefining what it means to be energy-resilient, digital-first and development-driven. While facing some of the most acute climate and energy vulnerabilities, they are turning digitalization into a catalyst for just energy transitions. 
  
More than 60% of SIDS import over 90% of their fossil fuels, resulting in energy costs up to four times higher than those in continental regions. Despite these structural challenges, many SIDS are setting ambitious climate targets, including 100% renewable energy by 2030 and net-zero emissions by 2050 - a bold shift toward resilience, self-reliance, and economic transformation. 
  
Digital innovation is helping SIDS leapfrog traditional energy systems and transform access: 
 
🔋 Fiji, Palau, and Kiribati are pioneering smart energy management through the Smart Islands Project—boosting grid resilience and enabling remote, low-cost electrification. 
 
📊 Guyana is scaling digital connectivity with over 200 ICT hubs, empowering Indigenous communities with data access for local energy planning. 
 
📡 Kenya’s Energy Access Explorer is now being adapted to island contexts, using geospatial AI to guide investment and electrification strategies. 
 
By fusing digital intelligence with decentralized renewables, SIDS are unlocking new models of energy equity, resilience and sustainable development. With the right investments in open data, smart infrastructure, and local capacity, these “digital islands” can lead the way for the Global South.  
 
To see other success stores and find out how else SIDS are redefining development pathways, I  invite you to read this UNDP  Policy Paper: 👉 go.undp.org/34Q

What if integrating renewables wasn’t just about cutting carbon - but also saving lives? 
 
Every year, air pollution from energy systems causes 6.4 million premature deaths, with the greatest burden falling on women and children in low- and middle-income countries. Power generation, cooking, transport, and waste burning all contribute to a silent epidemic - with energy and related sectors together responsible for over 70% of global GHG emissions.  Yet digitally powered solutions are already helping make energy and transport systems more efficient; reducing both emissions and their health impacts: 👉 https://lnkd.in/eNH_Vefp
  
While 666 million people still live without electricity and 2.1 billion rely on polluting cooking fuels, the global energy-health crisis is also a moment of powerful opportunity. Across the Global South, countries are demonstrating that integrating renewables, powered by digital innovation, can simultaneously reduce emissions and deliver major health gains: 
 
🌱 Kenya is using geospatial tools like Energy Access Explorer to plan hybrid grid-extension and distributed renewables, improving rural access and air quality. 
 
🌱 India is optimizing microgrids with AI to better match demand with renewable supply - reducing fossil fuel use and energy waste. 
 
🌱 Trinidad and Tobago is pursuing wind energy and green hydrogen, shifting away from fossil-powered generation that fuels both pollution and illness. 
  
Digital technologies like IoT sensors, AI forecasting, and remote monitoring also help utilities manage grid stability and enhance energy efficiency – reducing energy use in buildings and transport by around 10–15% while accelerating a healthier energy transition in real time. 
 
This isn’t just energy action; it’s a pathway to cleaner air, stronger health systems and more resilient communities. 
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #AirQuality #DigitalForDevelopment #HealthAndEnergy

Grateful for the opportunity to join colleagues at @UNDPChina country office to to discuss how our new UNDP Strategic Plan 2026–2029 puts sustainable energy at the center of development; not just as an enabler, but as a strategic lever for shifting the development curve itself. 

China’s experience shows why this matters. With 47% of global wind & solar; 20M EVs (half the global fleet); and having already achieved its 2030 renewables target six years early, China is proving that transitions can be nationally transformative and globally catalytic. But ultimately, this is not only about megawatts; it is about people, communities and systems for shared prosperity. 

In our dialogue, I shared three priorities for deepening China’s leadership and expanding shared progress: 

🔹 South–South and triangular cooperation
With 25 regional projects totaling 12 GW of new capacity worth $5B under the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, and partnerships across Africa, Asia and the Pacific, China is extending its leadership. The next step is moving from projects to scalable solutions grounded in governance, safeguards and inclusion. 

🔹 Digital, data & AI for energy systems
With grid investment projected at $100B annually and data center demand set to nearly double to 945 TWh by 2030, China is pioneering AI forecasting, digital twins and open data. Embedding these innovations into just transition frameworks is essential to ensure they deliver inclusive benefits 

🔹 Energy as a lever for human development 
As set out in the new Strategic Plan, success will not be measured only in megawatts, but in human outcomes: schools and clinics with reliable power; farmers with modern tools; households with clean cooking; and communities with greater resilience to crisis. 

At UNDP  we are proud to work alongside China and global partners to connect innovation with governance, finance, and inclusion. A just energy transition is not only a national achievement – it's a shared global responsibility. The real challenge is not how fast we expand renewables, but how effectively we connect them to the people who need them most. 

#EnergyForDevelopment #EnergyTransition #JustTransition #China

⚡️Renewables are out-investing fossil fuels—cheaper than ever!
Such an honour to serve my third year on the UN Council of Engineers for the Energy Transition (#CEET) and to attend the Annual Forum, hosted by the GEIDCO(Global Energy Interconnection Development and Cooperation Organization) alongside the #GlobalInterconnectedConference 2025 (#CNCC, Beijing). 🙏 Heartfelt thanks to our Chinese colleagues at #CEET and #GEIDCO for the warm hospitality and remarkable experiences.
The forum opened with a welcome from Isaac Elizondo Garcia, remarks by Mr Ciyong ZOU (UNIDO) and Mr Cheng Zhiqiang (#GEIDCO), followed by reflections from Semida Silveira and ULF Larsson (CEET new co-chair). The tone echoed the UN Secretary-General’s call for a “supercharged surge” in renewables: investment now exceeds fossil fuels, and costs are lower—e.g., recent figures show solar PV ~41% cheaper and offshore wind ~53% cheaper than fossil fuel generation.
A highly experienced and motivating panel followed with Mr Riad Meddeb (UNDP), Mr James Wahogo (Eastern African Power Pool), Mr Hongpeng Liu (#UNESCAP), Ms Divya Kottadiel (Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL)), Mr Pedro Jatobá (GEIDCO, Brazil), and Professor Dr. Phoebe Koundouri (#SDSN).
Key takeaways
- Put people first: energy access, jobs, health, gender equity, and resilience must anchor every decision.
- Close the finance gap: de-risking, Energy Transition & Investment Plans, and performance-based models can unlock scale.
- Think regional: interconnected grids, shared planning, and standards cut costs and boost resilience.
- Don’t overlook clean cooking & distributed solutions: huge health and development gains.
- Universities & networks (e.g., SDSN): force multipliers for skills, data, and visibility.
I was glad to contribute to two high-impact levers:
- Energy conservation & efficiency—the fastest, cheapest first fuel.
- Circular economy—direct and indirect GHG cuts across value chains. As Circular Economy Engagement Coordinator with The SMEP Programme at UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD), I shared our Bangladesh textiles case on circular wastewater reuse, which drew strong interest. Full report: https://lnkd.in/gYie9HRW 
We also caught a glimpse of China’s rapid robotics advances—from agile “robot dogs” to boxing-capable humanoids—signalling a new era that can support (and challenge) how we work.
Now, time to recharge for tomorrow’s Global Interconnected Conference 2025. Special thanks to Frank, Shuguang Qi, and all local colleagues for making the event so special—and a big shout-out to our CEET online participants whose late-night dedication was truly inspiring.

It was a real pleasure to meet with my friend Dr. Gloria Magombo, Permanent Secretary for Energy and Power Development in Zimbabwe, to reflect on how Zimbabwe can accelerate its energy transition in ways that put people, resilience, and prosperity at the center.
 
Our discussion touched on three priorities that are vital to unlocking this transformation:
 
🇿🇼 Supporting Zimbabwe’s National Clean Cooking Strategy With nearly 62% of the population still without access to clean cooking, and rural access below 10%, the new National Clean Cooking Strategy is more than an energy plan. It is a health plan, a gender equality plan, and an environmental plan. UNDP stands ready to support its implementation with policy expertise, innovative finance and local delivery models.
 
🇿🇼 Mission 300 Zimbabwe’s ambitious compact under Mission 300, targeting 100% electricity access by 2030 and raising clean cooking access to 70%, is a milestone moment. Building on our Solar for Health and mini-grid initiatives, UNDP  is committed to helping ensure these targets translate into real, reliable services for households, clinics, schools and enterprises.
 
🇿🇼 South–South cooperation and financial instruments Closing Zimbabwe’s annual energy gap - which currently costs the country 6.1% of GDP - requires innovative finance and regional collaboration. Instruments like the Renewable Energy Fund show how blended finance and South–South learning can unlock scale and inclusion.
 
Zimbabwe’s journey shows that energy is not only a national priority, it is a shared responsibility. By linking ambition with action, and innovation with inclusion, we can ensure the transition delivers for those who need it most.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #CleanCooking #Mission300 #SouthSouthCooperation #Zimbabwe

⚡️ Harnessing digitalization & AI - Smart technologies can unlock grid capacity and optimize systems, but their true value lies in ensuring the transition is faster and fairer.
 
At @UNDP, our new Strategic Plan 2026–2029 positions energy as a strategic lever for shifting the development curve. With sustainable energy projects across 131 countries, we are already proving that the transition can be faster, fairer, and more transformative for people’s lives.
 
The technologies exist. The financing can be mobilized. The real challenge, and our shared responsibility, is ensuring no one is left behind.

It was a real pleasure to deliver the keynote at the Capacity Building and Training Parallel Forum: Advancing Global Carbon Neutrality Goals through Capacity Building. 

The momentum is undeniable: in 2024, renewables accounted for 92.5% of all new power generation, global clean energy investment surpassed $2.1 trillion, (more than double fossil fuels), and the renewable energy sector now supports 16 million jobs worldwide — with the potential to reach 40 million by 2050.  

But to turn this momentum into lasting impact, we must close the gap in capacity - the systems, skills and institutions that transform ambition into action: 

1️⃣ Investing in institutions & people - Every dollar invested in governance and skills can unlock tenfold in climate and energy finance. From Zimbabwe’s lithium policy to India’s incentives creating nearly 1M jobs, capacity is what translates ambition into investment and livelihoods. 

2️⃣ Scaling South–South & regional cooperation - Cooperation multiplies results. The African Continental Free Trade Area could unlock $9B annually, while lithium alliances in Latin America and nickel policies in Asia show how shared standards and supply chains accelerate progress. 

3️⃣ Leveraging innovation responsibly - From AI making grids 30% more efficient to monitoring systems hundreds of times faster, innovation is reshaping our energy systems in real-time. But to close divides rather than widen them, it must remain inclusive, affordable and people-centered. 

Carbon neutrality is not only a technological challenge. It depends on institutions, skills, finance and cooperation — and embedding capacity building into every layer of the transition. The opportunities are immense, if we choose to seize them. 

#EnergyForDevelopment #CarbonNeutrality #CapacityBuilding #SouthSouthCooperation #Innovation

"Financing is not an end in itself; the real measure is the development it delivers." 

This was at the heart of the dialogue that I co-convened with GEIDCO(Global Energy Interconnection Development and Cooperation Organization)  on “Bridging the Gap  Financing a Just and Inclusive Energy Transition.” 

We meet at a moment of paradox. Global clean energy investment will reach $2.2 trillion this year, yet less than 15% flows to developing economies outside China, and Africa, with its vast renewable potential, receives only 2% of that total. The challenge is not if the transition will be financed, but how - and whether it will be just, inclusive, and development-maximizing. From our panel session, three priorities came through strongly: 

🌏 Closing the financing gap through Southern leadership
From Africa’s green industrialization agenda to Asia-Pacific’s blended finance models, countries are already pioneering ambitious national strategies. The task now is to scale and aggregate pipelines to attract capital at the level required. 

🌏 De-risking & financial innovation as drivers of scale  
Sovereign green bonds in Indonesia, sukuk in the Middle East, and guarantee facilities in Africa show how innovative instruments can unlock billions. The next step is replication and mainstreaming. 

🌏 Maximizing development impact through energy investments  
Solarizing clinics in Zimbabwe, electrifying schools in Fiji, and powering farms in Bangladesh show how people-centered finance delivers. The task now is to scale these models so development outcomes define success. 

Grateful to Khaled Sharbatly , @Wang Yao, Pradeep Kurukulasuriya  Kurukulasuriya, @Yan Jing, and @Cheng Lin for their insights, and to @Beate Trankmann for reminding us that speed without fairness risks leaving people behind. 

At @UNDP, we believe the energy transition will only succeed if it delivers for people first: lighting homes, powering schools and opening opportunities across the Global South.

#EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #SustainableFinance #EnergyTransition

How can we navigate the green hydrogen pathways to drive energy resilience, industrial transformation, and inclusive growth across Asia-Pacific? And is this financially viable to deliver truly transformative change for our societies?
 
Today, I am delighted to co-convene, together with colleagues from @GEIDCO, a high-level dialogue at the 2025 Global Energy Interconnection Conference in Beijing. Our focus will be on how Asia-Pacific can lead the transition in ways that deliver inclusive growth, industrial transformation, and energy resilience.
 
I will be joined by @Yu Zhuoping, @Amir Lebdioui, @Zhu Yongsheng, @Wang Ju, and @Zhang Jinxuan. Together, we will explore how the region can advance the hydrogen transition; balancing domestic needs, export ambitions, and inclusive development.

Financing the Blue Economy involves a combination of private and public capital, often channeled through specialized financial instruments like blue bonds and blended finance mechanisms. This includes integrating blue economy criteria into existing financial systems, supporting blue economy activities through targeted investments in sectors like sustainable fisheries and renewable energy, and using ocean-focused financial products such as blue bonds, debt-for-nature swaps, and impact investing. Achieving this, requires collaboration between governments, financial institutions, and corporations to establish clear standards, transparent governance, and a strategic shift in capital allocation towards ocean health and economic growth. 

In a recent article, Belinda Bramley points to the critical role of banks in encouraging and then enabling investors to finance Blue Economy initiatives. As an example, she points to Asian Development Banks new incubator, which supports sovereign and corporate borrowers who have plans to offer blue bonds. In a keynote address at an event in 2021, organised by the same bank, I was able to add insights based on my own experience.
Another example - still at a formative stage - is the World Bank's Blue Economy toolkit to establish a development framework that is clear and can be universally applied. Although the Blue Economy is still a relatively new concept, and potential investors remain wary of committing the very large sums that are called for, there are different ways in which banks can help to build confidence. At different levels - international, regional, national and local - and from different sources of capital.
Bramley believes that banks can help to release much-needed investment. If the Blue Economy is to achieve its undoubted promise, much will depend on the ability of banks to achieve this.

Over and above the actions of different financial agencies, there is the underlying issue of a disparity between rich and poor nations. This is a theme which recurs throughout this book, reflecting the fact that the fulfilment of Blue Economy aspirations will fall well short if there is not a correcting mechanism to enable all parts of the world to invest.
Different nations have fallen behind in economic development, often through no fault of their own, and it is in the interests of all to
provide a more level playing field. The Blue Economy will not be achieved without this kind of recognition .

"Financing is not an end in itself; the real measure is the development it delivers."

🌏 Closing the financing gap through Southern leadership

🌏 De-risking & financial innovation as drivers of scale

🌏 Maximizing development impact through energy investments  
Solarizing clinics in Zimbabwe, electrifying schools in Fiji, and powering farms in Bangladesh show how people-centered finance delivers. The task now is to scale these models so development outcomes define success.

2️⃣ Embed safeguards: Large-scale hydrogen needs land, water, and minerals. Strong governance is vital to prevent water stress, land conflict, and inequality. 

3️⃣ Lead through cooperation: Regional partnerships on standards, infrastructure, and finance can amplify Asia-Pacific’s voice and build local value chains and skills. 

We explore these opportunities and trade-offs in more depth in our latest policy paper - Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen: 🔗 https://lnkd.in/e7f_tvA9 

At @UNDP, we believe the real promise of green hydrogen lies not in the technology alone, but in the choices we make today to ensure it drives inclusive, sustainable development for all.

The much-awaited UNDP report mapping the extractivist traps, technological risks and developmental opportunities from #GreenHydrogen is finally out. 

As things stand, the green hydrogen economy risks reinforcing historical extractive patterns and heightened exposure of developing nations to tech disruptions, while failing to deliver broad-based development benefits. 

This report 'NAVIGATING THE CURRENTS OF GREEN HYDROGEN', published in collaboration with the TIDE Centre, University of Oxford, and which I had the chance to co-write with Riad Meddeb and Pavel Bilek, proposes a “3P” framework - People, Planet, and Prosperity - to ensure that hydrogen strategies align with human development goals. 

For People: Projects must not consume renewable-based electricity for H2 exports that would otherwise be destined for local populations and instead bring energy additionality to expand energy access, build resilient electricity systems, and support labor upskilling to enable a just transition. 

For the Planet, we must avoid a decarbonization that leads to other types environmental degradation. Governments need strong internal environmental appraisal and regulations to address GH2 risks around land, water, biodiversity, and intense critical minerals use. Such regulations help avoid adverse environmental impacts and social injustices in the communities and ecosystems where GH2 is produced.

For Prosperity, though many countries seek to position themselves as first movers in the green hydrogen sector (Chile, Namibia, etc.), given the uncertainty surrounding future market demand and the rapid pace of technological disruptions, a cautious experimental approach may be more appropriate for many fiscally-constrained developing nations, where lessons from early entrants can inform more cost-effective and scalable hydrogen development strategies at more mature stages of the hydrogen learning curve. Governments must integrate hydrogen into strong technology foresight assessments and a coherent industrial policy to promote local value addition while guarding against technological obsolescence.  

Ultimately, green hydrogen is not a development guarantee but a policy choice. 

Read the full report here: https://lnkd.in/e63jWxgb

Without deliberate safeguards, the green hydrogen economy risks reinforcing historical extractive models, and exposing first mover nations to lost investments without the right guidance on technologies and pathways.

The policy paper introduces a 3P Framework—People, Planet, Prosperity to ensure strategies deliver inclusive development:
🔹 People: Expand energy access, upskill the workforce, and support a just transition.
🔹 Planet: Safeguard land, water, biodiversity, and minerals through strong governance.
🔹 Prosperity: Integrate hydrogen into industrial policy, foster local value chains, and phase investments.
 
This report offers practical policy levers for countries to steer green hydrogen at the right speed, time, and direction. With transparent governance and context-specific strategies, it can become a driver of just transitions and shared prosperity.

Mission 300 Development Partners Coordination Group: Aligning for Impact

Africa stands at an inflection point. Nearly 600 million people still live without electricity, yet the tools to close this gap—renewables, innovative finance, and new delivery models—are scaling faster than ever. The challenge is no longer just ambition, but delivery at pace and scale.

At today’s inaugural meeting of the Mission 300 Development Partners Coordination Group (DPCG), convened by the The World Bank Group  and the African Development Bank Group, I shared four key priorities that are essential to make Mission 300 a reality:

⚡ Joint forces for technical assistance and policy alignment: Coordinated support must go hand in hand with clear methodologies for measuring results, ensuring that productive energy use and clean cooking are fully embedded in national strategies.

⚡ Financial innovation and policy de-risking: Unlocking private capital at scale requires building bankable pipelines and sharing risk. UNDP  working with United Nations Capital Development Fund (UNCDF)  is advancing solutions to crowd in investment through guarantee schemes and blended finance mechanisms. Through the Africa Minigrid Programme, UNDP is supporting governments to create new regulatory frameworks and conduct Derisking Renewable Energy Investment (DREI) analyses—a strategic complement to other initiatives such as AfDB’s Africa Mini-Grids Market Acceleration Programme (AMAP).

⚡ Compact Delivery and Monitoring Units (CDMUs): Turning commitments into impact requires strong local ownership. UNDP is supporting CDMUs in Congo, Ethiopia, Tanzania, and Mozambique through the Italy-supported Energy for Growth Initiative, helping accelerate delivery on the ground by identifying pipelines of bankable projects.

At @UNDP, our strength lies in country presence, convening power, and delivery capacity. By joining forces with partners, we can transform ambition into reality—accelerating Africa’s energy transition and ensuring no one is left behind.

Carbon-Free Energy: Keeping up momentum on corporate commitments

Corporate ambition for carbon-free energy is higher than ever. Over 40% of the world’s largest 2,000 companies have net-zero pledges, covering more than 90% of the global economy. The challenge is no longer ambition; but turning pledges into action that is inclusive, transformative and delivers real impact.

At today’s @SEforALL convening during New York Climate Week, I had the pleasure of opening the session with a keynote, where I highlighted three priorities to move corporate climate commitments from ambition to action:

1️⃣ Smarter integration of AI and clean energy: Globally, AI-enabled systems could reduce electricity demand by up to 10% by 2030. In India, smart meters are already cutting distribution losses by 20%, while Brazil is advancing clean power-shoring to relocate industries to renewable hubs and cut emissions by up to 40%.

2️⃣ Scaling clean energy investment in the Global South: Sovereign green bonds in Bolivia and Chile and corporate PPAs in India & Kenya are already showing what’s possible. Scaling these models across Africa and Asia could unlock tens of gigawatts of new renewable capacity.

3️⃣ Going beyond emissions reduction: Net-zero must deliver jobs, resilience and equity. From Paraguay’s e-bus fleets to Rwanda’s solar irrigation with electric cargo bikes - boosting crop yields by 25% - clean energy and e-mobility are already transforming communities.

At @UNDP, we believe net-zero will only succeed if it is also just. Corporate climate action must go beyond compliance checklists to strategies that build competitiveness, resilience, and equity.

Can AI help power a Just Energy Future?

Today, we stand at a crossroads. ChatGPT now reaches over 400 million weekly users, yet 1.18 billion people still live without reliable energy access. This paradox highlights both the promise and the peril of AI: it can deepen divides, or it can help us build more efficient, resilient and equitable energy systems.

In this piece, co-written with my colleague Stefano Pistolese , we argue that a new paradigm, “planetary intelligence” is emerging. By learning from nature and managing systems holistically, AI has the potential to transform not just energy, but the interconnected challenges of water, land, biodiversity and culture. To seize this opportunity, we must act on three fronts:

1️⃣ Move from biomimicry to “machine ecology”: AI can shift from copying nature’s designs to managing energy like an ecosystem. Smart grids already cut losses by 20%, and predictive tools balance renewables in real time. At scale, this could cut emissions 10% by 2030 and expand access.

2️⃣ Scale ecosystem-level solutions: AI modeled on natural systems can manage trade-offs across water, land, and biodiversity, creating up to $1.3 trillion in value by 2030 while safeguarding planetary health.

3️⃣ Ground innovation in equity: Efforts like Masakhane’s 40 African language models show how planetary intelligence can reflect diverse cultures, widening who benefits from AI and ensuring inclusion in the energy transition.

The question is not if AI will reshape our energy future, but how - and whether it will do so in a way that serves all people, not just a few. With the right governance, AI can become a catalyst for just and sustainable development.

“SDG7 is not just one goal among many. It is the gateway to the entire 2030 Agenda.”

Together with distinguished colleagues – @Annika Blakstad Otterstedt, Rana Ghoneim , @Daniel Schroth, and @Fanny Missfeldt-Ringius – I had the privilege to moderate the session “Mobilizing a Final Push on SDG7 and Roadmap towards the 2026 HLPF Review.”

We met at a moment of paradox. Energy poverty is the single greatest constraint on development, yet 9 out of 10 dollars in clean energy still go to advanced economies and China. Meanwhile, 666 million people remain without electricity and 2.1 billion without clean cooking. This is not simply a financial imbalance, it is a developmental divide.

But it is also a moment of opportunity. Renewables, innovative finance, and new delivery models are scaling faster than ever – and the conversation is now evolving from compacts to implementation. Through initiatives like Mission 300, partners are joining forces to move from commitments to concrete action, accelerating delivery on the ground and ensuring energy access translates into better health, learning and opportunity

From our discussion, three imperatives came through strongly:

🙏 Reinvent cooperation With ODA falling by over 9% in 2024 and projected to decline further in 2025, traditional aid cannot close the gap. New coalitions and partnerships are needed to reach those left furthest behind.

⚡ Build resilient value chains Solar modules now cost just $0.10 per watt, but tariffs and fragmented supply chains risk eroding gains. Demand for lithium has quadrupled since 2015, yet Africa and Latin America still lack processing capacity - exporting resources while importing expensive technologies.

🌐 Leverage AI for inclusion Electricity demand from data centers and AI grew 20% in just two years, and could match the consumption of Canada and the UK by 2030. But AI can also optimize grids, cut losses of 20-25% in some countries, and unlock efficiency for universal access.

At @UNDP, we believe the energy transition must be measured not just in megawatts, but in lives transformed.

Clean Cooking: From overlooked issue to global priority

At today’s @UnitedNationsEnergy session on clean cooking, I was delighted to share why the clean cooking imperative must move from the margins of energy discussions to the center of sustainable development.

Every year, household air pollution from dirty cooking fuels causes 6.67 million deaths - more than malaria, tuberculosis and HIV/AIDS combined. The economic costs exceed $2.4 trillion annually, yet clean cooking receives < 1% of global energy investment, far below the $8 billion needed each year to reach universal access by 2030. We’re paying trillions to avoid spending billions.

To reframe this we must:

1️⃣ Integrate clean cooking into electrification planning – as is already happening in Zambia, where e-cooking is part of mini-grid expansion strategies, making entire systems more viable while supporting productive uses like food processing and irrigation.

2️⃣ Unlock innovative finance and market development – as is already happening in Tanzania, where the UNCDF-backed CookFund uses concessional loans and results-based finance to reduce end-user costs by up to 60%, proving that public capital can de-risk private investment and build viable markets.

3️⃣ Harness #digitalization, #AI, and IoT for innovation – as we are already seeing in Kenya, where IoT-enabled smart meters power pay-as-you-go LPG, letting households purchase fuel in $0.50 increments via mobile money, ensuring resilience even during COVID-19 lockdowns.

Momentum is building. The solutions are here. What’s missing is bold finance, political will and collective resolve.

#EnergyForDevelopment #CleanCooking #Health #SDG7 #climateweeknyc #unga80

The economic costs exceed $2.4 trillion annually, yet clean cooking receives < 1% of global energy investment, far below the $8 billion needed each year to reach universal access by 2030. We’re paying trillions to avoid spending billions.

To reframe this we must:

1️⃣ Integrate clean cooking into electrification planning – as is already happening in Zambia, where e-cooking is part of mini-grid expansion strategies, making entire systems more viable while supporting productive uses like food processing and irrigation.

2️⃣ Unlock innovative finance and market development – as is already happening in Tanzania, where the UNCDF-backed CookFund uses concessional loans and results-based finance to reduce end-user costs by up to 60%, proving that public capital can de-risk private investment and build viable markets.

3️⃣ Harness #digitalization, #AI, and IoT for innovation – as we are already seeing in Kenya, where IoT-enabled smart meters power pay-as-you-go LPG, letting households purchase fuel in $0.50 increments via mobile money, ensuring resilience even during COVID-19 lockdowns.

Momentum is building. The solutions are here. What’s missing is bold finance, political will and collective resolve.

Yesterday at a #UNGA80 side event on Data, Digital Transformation and the Resilience in the Energy Transition, I discussed a defining question for the AI era:
 
AI is already reshaping the #energy transition - but does it build resilience, or deepen fragility?

👉 Are we using #AI in a way that advances sustainable energy for all?
👉 How can we prevent AI from becoming another burden on already stressed systems, and instead ensure it can create real opportunities for development?
👉 Will we step up to govern our energy transitions, so they are not only resilient, but also just?
 
The answers will define whether AI accelerates the clean energy future - or becomes another burden on already fragile systems.
 
#UNGA #AI #EnergyTransition #Resilience #Sustainability

What is “planetary intelligence”?

In this new thought piece, Riad Meddeb and Stefano Pistolese define it as “the planet’s capacity to sustain habitable conditions through the integration of life, technology, and natural systems.”

It’s a powerful idea, with potential to catalyze a new paradigm in development - an ontological shift which sees our systems as interlinked and adaptive, with AI as a mirror to how nature processes complexity.

The AI future we are working to - optimizing energy systems in alignment with natural resource management - involves a global and distributed system of interconnected digital models, each based on a system of sensors and satellites, working to maximize human development potential while limiting climate impact. This sounds familiar, though, right? This is the same underlying logic of how our natural world functions. 

So, if “planetary intelligence” is to guide practice, let’s make sure we define it right. There are multiple lenses that can we use:

🔹 Planetary Intelligence as Distributed Cognition
Planetary intelligence isn’t a single brain, but millions of actors - from local communities to AI to forests and rivers - each contributing to resilience. Here, AI’s role is to amplify local decisions as part of a global network of feedback.

🔸 Planetary Intelligence as Optimizing within Boundaries
Intelligence as the ability to detect and respect limits - carbon budgets, water tables, biodiversity thresholds.

♦️ Planetary Intelligence as Temporal Feedback
Intelligence as the ability to link present actions with long-term planetary consequences. AI must embed ecological memory, ensuring decisions today safeguard generations to come.

How we define planetary intelligence will shape whether it remains a metaphor - or becomes a practical guide for the AI era.

Can AI help power a Just Energy Future?

Today, we stand at a crossroads. ChatGPT now reaches over 400 million weekly users, yet 1.18 billion people still live without reliable energy access. This paradox highlights both the promise and the peril of AI: it can deepen divides, or it can help us build more efficient, resilient and equitable energy systems.

In this piece, co-written with my colleague Stefano Pistolese , we argue that a new paradigm, “planetary intelligence” is emerging. By learning from nature and managing systems holistically, AI has the potential to transform not just energy, but the interconnected challenges of water, land, biodiversity and culture. To seize this opportunity, we must act on three fronts:

1️⃣ Move from biomimicry to “machine ecology”: AI can shift from copying nature’s designs to managing energy like an ecosystem. Smart grids already cut losses by 20%, and predictive tools balance renewables in real time. At scale, this could cut emissions 10% by 2030 and expand access.

2️⃣ Scale ecosystem-level solutions: AI modeled on natural systems can manage trade-offs across water, land, and biodiversity, creating up to $1.3 trillion in value by 2030 while safeguarding planetary health.

3️⃣ Ground innovation in equity: Efforts like Masakhane’s 40 African language models show how planetary intelligence can reflect diverse cultures, widening who benefits from AI and ensuring inclusion in the energy transition.

The question is not if AI will reshape our energy future, but how - and whether it will do so in a way that serves all people, not just a few. With the right governance, AI can become a catalyst for just and sustainable development.
